{{RunningHeader|this|6296|thistle-down}}{{smaller block|From the town you last came through, called Brailsford, it is five miles; and you are not yet above half a mile on ''this side.'' {{right|''Cotton'', in Walton's Angler, ii. 222.}}}} {{smaller block|(''b'') Time just past or just at hand; the last or the next. The reference, whether to past or to future, is determined by the circumstances; ''this evening'' may mean either the evening now approaching, or next to come, or the evening now present, or the evening just past: as, it has occurred twice ''this'' year; I shall take care not to fail ''this'' (next) time. In this connection ''this'' is sometimes used for ''these'', the sum being reckoned up, as it were, in a total.}} {{smaller block|The owle ek, which that hette Ascaphilo,
Hath efter me shright al ''this'' nyghtes two. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, v. 320.}}}} {{smaller block|I learn'd in Worcester, as I rode along,
He cannot draw his power ''this'' fourteen days. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iv. 1. 126.}}}} {{smaller block|I have not wept ''this'' forty years; but now
My mother comes afresh into my eyes. {{right|''Dryden'', All for Love, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|[In Shakspere the phrase ''this night'' occurs, meaning ''last night.''}} {{smaller block|''Glouc.'' My troublous dream ''this night'' doth make me sad.
''Duch.'' What dream'd my lord? tell me, and I'll requite it
With sweet rehearsal of my morning's dream. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., i. 2. 22.]}}}} '''This . . . here.''' See ''here''1.—'''This other†''', the other. {{smaller block|And hem liked more the melodye of this harpour than eny thinge that ''this other'' mynstralles diden. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 621.}}}} {{smaller block|You denied to fight with me ''this other'' day. {{right|''Shak.'', W. T., v. 2. 140.}}}} '''This present.''' See ''present''1. '''II.''' ''pron.'' This person or thing. {{smaller|(''a'') It denotes—Some person or thing actually present or at hand: as, is ''this'' your coat? Who is ''this?''}} {{smaller block|''This'' is a spell against them, spick and span new. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Bartholomew Fair, iii. 1.}} Fie, what an idle quarrel is ''this''; was ''this'' her ring? {{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') Something that has just preceded or has been mentioned or referred to.}} {{smaller block|Alle ''thes'' were there wythoute fable, Wythoute ham of the rounde table. {{right|''Arthur'' (ed. Furnivall), l. 179.}}}} [[File:century v08 p0100 c1f1.png|center|78px]] {{c|Canada Thistle (''Cr'' ''arvensis'').}} {{c|Upper part of stem heads; ''a'', a flower achene with pappus}} {{smaller block|When they heard ''this'' [the discourse of Peter] they were pricked in their hearts. {{right|Acts ii. 37.}}}} {{smaller block|Suetonius writes that Claudius found heer no resistance, and that all was done without stroke; but ''this'' seems not probable. {{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., ii.}}}} {{smaller block|I know no evil which touches all mankind so much as ''this'' of the misbehaviour of servants. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 88.}}}} (''c'') Emphatically, something that is to be immediately said or done: as, Let me tell you ''this:'' I shall lend you no more money. {{smaller block|But know ''this'', that if the goodman of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched, and would not have suffered his house to be broken up. {{right|Mat. xxiv. 43.}}}} (''d'') Elliptically, this person, place, state, time, position, circumstance, or the like: as, I shall leave ''this'' [place or town] to-morrow; ''this'' [state of affairs] is very sad; I shall abstain from wine from ''this'' [time] on; by ''this'' [time] we had arrived at the house. {{smaller block|''This'' [that is, this one] is so gentil and so tendre of herte That with his deth he wol his sorwes wreke. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iii. 904.}}}} {{smaller block|I shall, between ''this'' and supper, tell you most strange things from Rome. {{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iv. 3. 43.}}}} {{smaller block|By ''this'' the vessel half her course had run. {{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Ovid's Metamorph., x. 95.}}}} When opposed to ''that'', ''this'' refers to the person or thing that is nearer, ''that'' to the person or thing that is more distant; so, with things that have just been expressed, ''this'' refers to the thing last mentioned (and therefore nearer in time to the speaker), and ''that'' to the thing first mentioned (as being more remote). {{smaller block|Two ships from far making amain to us: Of Corinth ''that'', of Epidaurus ''this''. {{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., i. 1. 94.}}}} {{smaller block|A body of ''this'' or ''that'' denomination is produced. ''Boyle.''}} {{smaller block|''These'' will no taxes give, and ''those'' no pence; Critics would starve the poet, Whigs the prince. {{right|''Dryden'', Prol. to Southern's Loyal Brother, l. 10.}}}} {{smaller block|Some place the bliss in action, some in ease, ''Those'' call it pleasure, and contentment ''these''. {{right|''Pope'', Essay on Man, iv. 22.}}}} ''This'' is sometimes opposed to ''the other''. {{smaller block|Consider the arguments which the author had to write ''this'', or to design ''the other'', before you arraign him. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}} It was sometimes used elliptically for ''this is.'' {{smaller block|''This'' 'a good Fryer, belike. {{right|''Shak.'', M. for M.
